big: Meena has no employer pension. She wants a retirement account she opens herself, with low costs and a choice of how it is invested. NPS was built for people like her.

lines: In NPS, who decides where my money goes?
You do, within limits. You pick how much goes to equity, bonds and government securities, or let an automatic option shift it by age.

rows: The main retirement account, with rules on withdrawal
A flexible account, with no such restrictions
How much goes to equity, bonds and government securities
A pension bought with part of the pot at exit
note: NPS is regulated by PFRDA. The exact exit rules are set by PFRDA and can change, so check the current ones.

title: About NPS
stops: Tier I is the main retirement account
NPS lets you pick how the money is invested
You can take out the whole pot at exit, with no pension
NPS is run by the bank you save with
caps: Tier I holds your long-term retirement money, with withdrawal rules.
Within limits, you choose the mix, or use an automatic life-stage option.
A set part of the pot must buy an annuity at exit, under PFRDA rules.
NPS is regulated by PFRDA, and not run by a single bank.

q: Rohan wants his NPS to move towards safer assets as he nears retirement, without his involvement. What suits him?
opts: A fixed choice of all equity for good
Using Tier II as the main pot
why: All equity for the whole period does not reduce risk near retirement.
Closing the account each year would break the long-term plan.
An automatic option shifts the mix with age, so he does not need to.
Tier II is flexible, but it is not meant to be the main retirement pot.

q: Meena reaches NPS exit age. What must she do with part of the pot?
opts: Use a set share to buy an annuity
Hand it all over to the government
Reinvest all of it in shares
Leave it idle for another ten years
why: The rules require part of the pot to buy an annuity, a regular pension.
The pot belongs to her, and it is not handed over in full to anyone.
No rule demands reinvesting it all in shares.
Idle money does not meet the rule, which asks for an annuity.

q: A friend says NPS Tier I and Tier II are the same. What is the difference?
opts: Tier I is for the old, and Tier II for the young
Tier II must be kept for sixty years
There is no difference between them
Tier I has withdrawal rules, and Tier II is flexible
why: Age does not decide the tier. The purpose and the rules do.
Tier II has no such lock, so it is the flexible one.
The tiers differ in how freely money can be taken out.
Tier I is the main retirement account with rules. Tier II is flexible.

q: Who regulates the National Pension System?
why: SEBI regulates securities markets and not the pension system.
PFRDA is the pension regulator that oversees NPS in India.
IRDAI regulates insurers and is not the pension regulator.
An employer may offer NPS, but it does not regulate it.

pts: NPS is a voluntary pension account regulated by PFRDA.
Tier I is the main account. Tier II is flexible.
A set part of the pot must buy an annuity. Check the current exit rules.
